structure.title: Clarifying the principle
structure.text: Early chapters explain utility and respond to the charge that a morality of happiness is shallow or merely selfish.

structure.title: Motivation and justice
structure.text: Later chapters consider moral commitment, the principle's justification, and the special force of justice.

people.name: Utility
people.text: Mill's principle that actions are right in so far as they tend to promote happiness, meaning pleasure and freedom from pain, for everyone affected.

people.name: Higher pleasures
people.text: Mill's claim that some pleasures, of the mind and of feeling, are worth more than others, so that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

people.name: Justice
people.text: The obligations people feel most strongly, which critics said utility could not explain, and which Mill tries to account for in his last chapter.

context.title: Everyone's happiness
context.text: The standard includes other people's welfare, not merely the agent's advantage. Conflicts between interests are therefore internal to the account.
context.takeaway: Count whose welfare enters the argument.

context.title: Quality and quantity
context.text: Mill argues that pleasures can differ in kind and value. This complicates the image of a simple sum of agreeable sensations.
context.takeaway: The theory must explain its comparisons.

notice.text: Follow objections before Mill answers them.
notice.why: They show what the principle is being asked to preserve.

notice.text: Notice the account of rights and security.
notice.why: Justice is not dismissed merely because consequences matter.

opening: If an action makes people's lives better, that seems a powerful reason to do it. Trouble begins when one person's happiness comes at another's expense, or when a satisfying life requires more than accumulating pleasures. Mill takes the apparently simple idea that morality should serve happiness and works through its most troublesome implications. Justice, sacrifice, and the quality of enjoyment become tests of whether a principle meant to take everyone's welfare seriously can explain the obligations people are least willing to trade away.
